title: Quadratic-form order and positive operators
subtitle: G2 lecture 033000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded companion deck developed from the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix. Adds explicit mathematical formulas, worked examples, and topic-specific diagrams while remaining standalone.

slides.title: Energy as a quadratic form
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 033000 · Energy as a quadratic form
slides.lead: A self-adjoint operator is called positive when it never assigns negative energy to a vector.
body: For a self-adjoint matrix A, the scalar ⟨Ax,x⟩ is the quadratic form determined by A. Positivity means this scalar is at least zero for every vector x.
Thinking in terms of quadratic forms is more flexible than staring at entries. It behaves well under changes of basis, compression to subspaces, and spectral decomposition.
slides.takeaway: Positivity is a geometric property of the quadratic form, not a statement about entrywise signs.

slides.title: Definition of positivity
slides.lead: For self-adjoint A, positivity is tested on every vector.
body: The definition makes sense because self-adjointness guarantees the quadratic form is real-valued. If A were not self-adjoint, ⟨Ax,x⟩ could be complex and the inequality would not even be meaningful.
Later the notation A ≤ B will mean B − A ≥ 0, so positivity is the basic building block of operator order.
slides.takeaway: Quadratic-form inequalities require self-adjoint operators from the start.

slides.title: Negative entries can still produce a positive operator
slides.lead: Entrywise signs do not decide positivity.
body: For x = (u,v), the quadratic form equals u² − 2uv + v² = (u−v)², which is always nonnegative. So a matrix with negative off-diagonal entries may still be positive.
This example is a warning: positivity is about the entire quadratic expression, not about every individual coefficient being nonnegative.
slides.takeaway: The quadratic form sees cancellation that entrywise inspection can miss.

slides.title: Spectral criterion for positivity
slides.lead: For self-adjoint operators, positivity is equivalent to spectral nonnegativity.
body: If A has an orthonormal eigenbasis, then ⟨Ax,x⟩ becomes a weighted average of the eigenvalues with nonnegative weights |c_i|². So all eigenvalues nonnegative implies positivity.
Conversely, an eigenvector for a negative eigenvalue would make the quadratic form negative on that vector. Thus positivity and nonnegative spectrum coincide in finite dimensions.
slides.takeaway: The spectral theorem turns positivity into a simple statement about eigenvalues.

slides.title: Ordering two operators
slides.lead: Once positivity is defined, comparison is defined by subtraction.
body: This means ⟨Ax,x⟩ ≤ ⟨Bx,x⟩ for every vector x. The order is partial, not total: two self-adjoint operators need not be comparable.
Still, this order is powerful because it lets us convert spectral placement, compressions, and Gram constructions into inequalities that are valid on every vector.
slides.takeaway: Operator order means uniform quadratic-form domination over all vectors.

slides.title: Order survives changes of coordinates and compression
slides.lead: Positive operators stay positive under natural geometric operations.
body: If U is unitary, then U*AU has the same quadratic form values after a change of coordinates, so positivity is preserved. Likewise, compressing A to a subspace keeps positivity because the restricted quadratic form is still nonnegative there.
These closure properties explain why positivity is the right language for invariant subspaces, blocks, and projections.
slides.takeaway: Positivity is intrinsic and survives standard coordinate-free constructions.

slides.title: Gram operators are automatically positive
slides.lead: For any linear map T, the operator T* T is positive.
body: This is the prototypical positivity argument. The quadratic form of T* T is literally a squared norm, so nonnegativity is automatic.
Later, square roots of T* T give the modulus |T|, and the singular values of T are the square roots of the eigenvalues of this positive Gram operator.
slides.takeaway: Many important positive operators arise because they are Gram operators T* T.

slides.title: Products require care
slides.lead: Even if A and B are positive, the product AB need not be positive.
body: The reason is that AB may fail to be self-adjoint unless A and B commute. Without self-adjointness, positivity is not even defined in the same way. If A and B do commute, then simultaneous diagonalization shows AB is positive because it multiplies nonnegative spectral values.
So positivity behaves well under products only under an additional compatibility hypothesis.
slides.takeaway: Positivity is not closed under arbitrary multiplication; commutation matters.

slides.title: Why we care: square roots and modulus
slides.lead: Positive operators are exactly the ones on which canonical square roots make sense.
body: If A ≥ 0, then the scalar function t ↦ √t is defined on its spectrum, so the functional calculus produces a positive square root. For a general map T, positivity of T* T gives the modulus |T| = (T* T)^{1/2}.
That is why positivity is not merely a side topic. It is the gateway to the operator constructions needed for singular values and polar decomposition.
slides.takeaway: Positivity is the doorway to canonical square roots, moduli, and singular-value theory.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.lead: Keep the quadratic-form viewpoint in front of you.
body: A positive operator is a self-adjoint operator whose quadratic form is never negative. The spectral theorem turns that into the condition σ(A) ⊆ [0,∞). Operator order is defined by positivity of differences, and Gram operators T* T are the canonical examples.
These ideas feed directly into positive square roots and the modulus of an operator.
slides.takeaway: Quadratic-form order is the right language for comparing self-adjoint operators.
